speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CO-OPERATION IN INDUSTRIAL APPLICATION OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA AND PROTOCOL AND PRESS RELEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 41 (2) and with the agreement of the House, I should like to table, in the two official languages, copies of the agreement between the governments of Canada and the U.S.S.R. on co-operation in the industrial application of science and technology, the protocol of the first meeting of the Canadian-Soviet Mixed Commission, as well as the communique issued at the end of those talks.
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of leading the Canadian delegation composed of civil servants and businessmen. The purpose of this visit was to sign the agreement referred to, and to hold the first meeting of the Canadian-Soviet Mixed Commission set up under the agreement.
We were greeted warmly, our discussions were constructive, and everything seems to indicate that they will lead to mutual benefits.
The agreement aims at encouraging co-operation between the two countries in the field of industrial science and technology. That co-operation could take the form of exchanges of information, and visits of businessmen and experts. It could also lead to licensing agreements in specific areas of technology.

It might lead to all kinds of "joint ventures". I suggest it will also lead to increases in two-way trade between the two countries.
Numerous meetings were held in Moscow between members of the Canadian delegation and their opposite numbers in various industrial and research sectors of the Soviet administration. These discussions identified a considerable range of subjects of mutual interest to the two countries. As a result, six working groups have been established in order to further identify prospects for mutually beneficial exchanges. The groups are as follows: architecture, construction and building materials; forest-based industry; non-ferrous metals industry; electric power industry; oil industry, and gas industry. Formation
of an additional group to consider airport design, facilities and servicing is under consideration.
Certain features which emerged from the discussion are worthy of special mention.
1.	Problems arising from severe climatic and permafrost conditions are of considerable interest to both countries and have been identified for study by the working groups in construction, electric power, the oil industry and the gas industry.
2.	The naming of the six working groups I have mentioned does not, of course, exhaust the area of possible co-operation in the industrial application of science and technology. In addition to working groups, other contacts will continue, and further working groups may be established by agreement.
I was impressed by the speed with which our Canadian businessmen and experts were able to get down to specifics with their Soviet counterparts.
The next session of the mixed commission will be held in Ottawa early in 1972.
While I was in Moscow I met separately with Mr. Patolichev, the Soviet Minister of Foreign Trade. We engaged in a useful review of trade developments and of prospects for the further expansion of trade. I was invited also to call on Mr. Polyansky, Deputy Premier of the Soviet Union. Our discussions covered the broad range of relationships between Canada and the Soviet Union. Mr. Polyansky particularly asked me to convey to the Governor General of Canada and to the Prime Minister the greetings of Mr. Podgorny, President of the Soviet Union, Premier Kosygin and First Secretary Brezhnev. He also asked me to tell the Canadian Prime Minister-and I do so now-how much the Soviet government is looking forward to welcoming him to the Soviet Union later this year.

speechtext:
I certainly appreciate the minister's courtesy in making a report to the House on his recent visit to Russia and on the series of meetings which were held during that visit. I think what was done will serve a very useful purpose.
The basic concept behind the whole mission is an arrangement whereby two states which have so much in common in terms of climatic condition and industrial development will be able to exchange ideas and information not only at the governmental level but at the industrial level. We note the minister's observation that the effectiveness of these meetings will be reviewed on an annual basis and that provision has been made for the setting up of further working committees if necessary. As

February 4, 1971
Trade Agreement with Russia
is so often the case, their success will depend to a great extent on the initiative shown by the Canadian business community and Canadian industry, encouraged, of course, by government action.
There is no doubt in our minds that the Russians will take full advantage of this agreement by sending over their experts and students to assimilate, as far as possible, any advantageous information which may have accrued from our development here in Canada. The onus is upon us to see that this interest is reciprocated and that we in turn take full advantage of the opportunities which are granted to us by the Russian government.
The minister told us of the meeting between himself and his Russian counterpart in the field of trade. I am sorry he was not able to go into more detail, because the Soviet Union is and can be an important buyer of Canadian grain, pulp and paper, and other exports; anything which can be done to encourage a still greater readiness on the part of the Soviet Union to purchase the commodities we have to offer will work to the great advantage of this country.
We welcome the minister's statement and the tabling of this agreement. We shall await with a great deal of interest the development of this new arrangement between the two countries.

subtopic: CO-OPERATION IN INDUSTRIAL APPLICATION OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA AND PROTOCOL AND PRESS RELEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) for having worked out these mechanisms for closer integration with the Soviet Union in respect of the exchange of information, technical know-how and trade. It is undoubtedly true that as nations learn to trade with each other there is a tendency for some of the tensions that can lead to conflict to be reduced. I think the minister has taken a very excellent first step in this direction.
When Your Honour's predecessor took a delegation of parliamentarians to the Soviet Union in 1965 we found that the Soviet Union was interested in a great many commodities which Canada produces. One of the main obstacles to trade was that they in turn wanted to sell in Canada so that they could pay for their purchases. I think that the machinery the minister has set up should make it possible for the Russians to find markets in Canada for goods that are competitive and this should enable them to purchase more Canadian products. I think the minister has taken an excellent first step and we hope that success will attend his efforts.

speechtext:

I refer to the complete disregard of the public interest in the Atlantic region which the railways have shown by taking advantage of the government's failure to work out its promised special transportation policy for the Atlantic region in the past two years, which has meant that in less than a year and a half freight rate increases have averaged 25 to 35 per cent and those on lumber as much as 40 per cent. speechtext:
I have now had an opportunity of examining the observations made by the minister yesterday in

February 4, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 answer to some questions I raised about quality standards as affected by mine tailings. I cannot but express surprise at the indication that the proposed ministry will play a very passive role when it comes to the application of the new provisions in the Fisheries Act, for whose administration the new department will be responsible.
As I understand it, the application of the relevant provision of the Act as amended last session in connection with the requirement for the submission of plans by industry, is to be left in abeyance. The minister suggested that his officers might keep the situation under surveillance and take action of some kind if the situation seemed to require it. However, apparently no provision is being made for any official approval or permission being given before a plant proceeds with its plans. He said no permit would be issued.
I think the minister fully appreciates the importance, indeed the urgency, of this question in relation to some of the mining developments that are taking place near the coastal waters of British Columbia. Certainly, he is aware of the developments at the north end of Vancouver Island on Quatsino Sound. I am sure also he knows about the application by Texada Mines, which I understand is before the pollution control board of British Columbia, with regard to the disposing of its effluent into the Strait of Georgia. This is an area very dear to the minister's heart, and he has been talking about having it made into a national park.
I wonder whether the minister could enlighten us a little further on the statements he made yesterday with regard to how he envisages the new department of the environment will control mine effluents in water areas. This question is important not only to the commercial fishery but also in respect of many other amenities such as recreation and the enjoyment of areas such as the Strait of Georgia.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has been asking whether we are taking advantage of the new provisions of the Fisheries Act to insist on information from mining companies relative to their plans for expansion. I hasten to assure him that this is the case. We are reviewing a dozen projects at the moment. In instances where we find there is not likely to be any damage to the fishery or to any other aspect of the marine ecology, we still reserve the right to prosecute if later the development is found to be of a different character than we had been led to expect or our own analysis turns out to be wrong.
I must hasten to add that we do not give permits to carry out a given operation, but we do insist on obtaining the plans and vetting the intentions of the company in question. We can ask for modifications, as was the case with the Utah Mining company in Quatsino Sound, and will always monitor the industry's operations to ensure that the aquatic environment is protected. This practice is being followed in a number of places across the country. For instance, in the Miramichi we are working with the mining industry, vetting its plans for expansion and
giving advice with a view to reducing hazards to fish life in that basin.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one further aspect I should like the minister to clarify. I am not in any way seeking to encourage any areas of difference between federal and provincial administrations; nevertheless, I think we are all aware that from time to time, as a result of different approaches and the existence of different legislation, federal and provincial, there may well be at times some difference of view.
One of the things that has been puzzling me is this. Let me take as an example the Quatsino Sound operation of Utah Construction and Mining, to which both the minister and I have made reference. I understand a permit has been issued in respect of that operation by the pollution control board of British Columbia. I also understand that, generally speaking, the plans which are being developed have, if not the blessing, at least the acquiescence of the Department of Fisheries. This development is taking place in what is undoubtedly an important fisheries area. In view of this, if a permit were issued by the provincial pollution control board under terms and conditions that required action to be taken to deal with the discharge of tailings but which, in the opinion of the minister and the department, were entirely inadequate as far as the protection of the environment and aquatic life were concerned, what kind of machinery would the minister envisage to resolve an impasse of this kind? The minister has mentioned that no permit would be issued; that the blessing of the department with regard to the specifications for carrying out the operation has priority over the decision of any provincial board in such an instance as this. Could the minister enlighten the committee in this regard?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is thinking of a specific instance on Canada's west coast-

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I intervene to say that I cited that only as an example. I am not suggesting there is any dispute in this regard; I am merely putting a hypothetical proposition to the minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, might I use the example that the hon. member brought forward to illustrate my point. My point is that there are federal provisions dealing with pollution in the west coast instance referred to, the Fisheries Act. There is also provincial legislation, the legislation setting up the provincial pollution control board. It is necessary for the company in question to comply with both pieces of legislation. While it is possible that this development would receive the full approval of the provincial authorities, it could still rim head-on into federal legislation, the regulations, for example, made pursuant to the federal Fisheries Act.
In the instance of the Utah Mining the company would have to do two things. It would have to satisfy the federal government, particularly with respect to the provisions of the federal Fisheries Act; it would also
LMr. Barnett.]

have to satisfy the rules laid down by the B.C. pollution control board. We have a good working arrangement with the B.C. pollution control board whereby, before it grants a permit, it has the application vetted by the federal department of fisheries regional office. We have had no instance within the last year or two of any provincial permit being granted without the scrutiny of and clearance by the federal fisheries people. We are working closely together. But in an imaginary case where the industry offends the Fisheries Act but somehow manages to gain the approval of the provincial control board, it, the industry, is still in trouble with the federal authorities.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Coming back, Mr. Chairman, to the minister's statement that no permit is issued, what evidence does an operating mining company have that in fact it has the approval of the federal authorities? Take the case of a mine development where, as matters stand, part of the ability of the firm to secure the necessary development financing hinges on federal approval of its operating plans. If there is no system of permits, what evidence does the mining company have that, in fact, the plans that it is proposing have the approval of the federal control authorities?
This is one of the administrative questions that arise in the development of this kind of legislation which I think is of interest and concern. I can see some important question being raised with regard to the ability to develop a resource as well as the ability of a company to give evidence to concerned citizens in the area that its plans have in fact been examined and approved.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the company would be unwise to proceed with its plans and to invest a substantial amount of money in a development which was likely to have an unfavourable impact on the local ecology without first having discussed it with our federal people in that area and having been satisfied that we saw no great difficulty in their planned proceedings. In situations where the provincial board also requires the approval of the federal authorities the industry should make doubly sure that our federal people are happy with the development and can see no major problem arising from it.
Of course, the federal department can step in and demand plans in cases where the company has not been cooperative in making its plans available, or neglects to make modifications which our engineers say should be made to protect the local environment. This is a matter involving disclosure, close liaison and frank advice on the part of the department. As I said, we do not approve of the project. The provincial authorities may give approval, but we reserve the right to move in at any time and to require further modification if there is any evidence of danger to the environment.

speechtext: Who or what section of the new department will be in a position to assess the ecological costs of different development programs throughout the country? I am thinking in terms of a hydro plant being built on some river. Are there powers under the minister's department to carry out an ecological survey in respect of the cost of these projects?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was one of those who said the fisheries service should be separated from the environment department. One of the capabilities which will be brought to bear on any hydro development in a fisheries river will be the staff of the federal fisheries service. We will also have the support of the biologists in our wildlife service and the engineers from the water sector of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. We will have the technical competence to assess the ecological consequences of hydro dams and other types of industrial development as well. One of the reasons for including the fisheries service in this new department is to include a biological competence to deal with the ecological aspects of industrial development.

Government Organization Act, 1970

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Might I just follow up with another question or two on this matter? The fisheries department has always been interested in navigable waters, and in a position to take a stand on anything that would have an effect on the fisheries in navigable streams. The point I am getting at is that Crown corporations which wish to build a hydro dam are not covered by the Navigable Waters Protection Act. They are answerable to no one, either provincially or federally. We are bringing the water resources branch into the new department but why are we not putting the Navigable Waters Protection Act under the jurisdiction of this new department? This is one of the things excluded in schedule A.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the simple answer is that the Navigable Waters Protection Act has to do with navigation and not ecology. If a hydro development were likely to interfere with navigation or the use of a river for that purpose, such an assessment would, I think, be made by the Department of Transport rather than a department dealing with the environment.
This is not to say we will not be concerned about the impact of that development on living resources, or about an industry which exploits the living resources of a stretch of river including fisheries, wildlife and, to the extent we have federal authority, forests and so on. We will be concerned about hydro development or any other project on a river, and we will have some views about navigation as well. Nevertheless, the administration of the Navigable Waters Protection Act should be a matter for the Department of Transport, not the department of environment. I think the hon. member sees this as a way of stopping pollution rather than protecting navigable waters for navigation. This Act is to protect Canadian waters from the point of view of navigation alone.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think this is one of the key points as far as studies of the ecology are concerned. I have in mind what might be done behind a hydro dam, for example. The Navigable Waters Protection Act prevents one from putting many types of pollution into a navigable water. However, the point I am coming to is that the minister's department will be helpless to do anything about the ecological damage which occurs behind a dam. The department will be able to make ecological surveys, but will not be able to do anything about the damage unless we make the Navigable Waters Protection Act applicable to Crown corporations in the name of the provinces or the federal government. I urge the minister to give serious consideration to this aspect.
As the minister knows, we have had several disasters in British Columbia. One occurred behind the Duncan Dam, where tens of thousands of acres of valuable tim-berland were flooded. This pollution problem will exist as long as we allow this type of thing. The Mica Dam on the Columbia River will create a lake 125 miles long, and none of the timber is to be cut before the area is flooded. Since this is a navigable stream, it is within federal jurisdiction. There must be some provision in the legislation which will force hydro authorities to clean up. We will not allow that type of pollution to exist. This is the point I am trying to make. We cannot allow this legislation to pass without some provision for checking on the type of development that has taken place all over Canada, not only in B.C. These are the things about which we are apprehensive. I urge the minister to attempt to insert into these acts-and the Navigable Waters Protection Act is one-a provision which will make Crown corporations subject to those acts.
I think the minister's department should call for ecological surveys to be carried out. If the cost of the damage behind the dam is so extensive that the project is not a paying proposition, we should turn thumbs down on the project and obtain power by other means. This is of vital interest to all sections of Canada. New dams will be built; some of them will start this year. We cannot let this situation go on any longer. Someone has to start surveying, and I suggest this new department should tackle it.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised an interesting point, but let me draw his attention to the Fisheries Act which enables us to do the very things that he has been mentioning. The Fisheries Act was amended in several ways last spring, that is in the spring of 1970. One way in which it was amended was to include Crown corporations and agencies, provincial and federal. We have used it against Manitoba hydro, requiring it to release water into the lower reaches of the Nelson River recently. We required Manitoba hydro to look after the ecology downstream of the big new dam at Kelsey on the Nelson River. We have done in Manitoba just the sort of thing that the hon. member is suggesting we do under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Under the Fisheries Act we can deal with pollution and directly. We do not have to use the pretext of navigation. We have the powers which he is asking us to use.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to draw to the minister's attention a recommendation by members in the Official Opposition in connection with the environmental council of Canada to which reference was made a few minutes ago by my hon. friend to the left. Earlier in the debate I referred to the report of the pollution probe conducted, under the auspices of the Leader of the Opposition, a document signed by one John A. Fraser and our colleague, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka who has been absent from this debate because of illness. The House will be pleased to know that he is recovering and we hope will be back with us very shortly. When a person of his calibre is missing there is a substantial loss to a debate like this.
I should like to quote, without very much embellishment because I am not as knowledgeable in this field as is the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, one of the recommendations of the pollution probe carried out under the auspices of the Leader of the Opposition.
Establish an environmental council of Canada, composed of a majority of members outside the government service, drawn from such organizations as citizens' anti-pollution groups, universities, industry, labour and conservation bodies, and with

February 4, 1971

government representation. The council would be provided with the necessary funds and facilities to advise the government and Parliament on environmental matters generally.
I have quoted word for word what is contained in that document. Since the minister is faced with the challenge of a new department and with some rather substantial problems indeed, some of which have been raised by me and some by other members during the debate, members on this side of the House as well as those on the minister's side would probably find it acceptable if he were to decide to take the plunge and establish an environmental council of Canada.
The only other point I would make to the minister, if he were to consider such a worthwhile step, is that he and the government pay more attention to such an environmental council's recommendations than the present government is now paying to the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Recently, a report of the International Joint Commission painted a pretty dim picture of the situation so far as the Great Lakes are concerned. I was pleased to learn yesterday during the debate that the minister is establishing national standards which will apply across Canada. I understood from his answer that the standards set by his department would be the yardstick so far as pollution levels across the country were concerned. I asked him yesterday about the Great Lakes and quoted from clause 5 which provides that his department is to enforce rules and regulations made by the International Joint Commission. The question is this: does the International Joint Commission have the necessary expertise in this particular field to make these recommendations? If they do, will we not be duplicating this service through the minister's new department? I am concerned that one day the International Joint Commission might make a regulation with which the minister had nothing to do other than to enforce it.
I respect the dedication of the minister, but I am afraid that he may wind up one day in a strait jacket, being told what to do by IJC and their regulations may not meet his standards. Is there not a chance that we will be duplicating services? Every time you do that you are just postponing the day when this problem will be solved. The more bodies we have, the more chance there is for a foul up.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The answer is that there is no overlapping and no duplication. The International Joint Commission is a very compact commission. In a sense, it is like a court, a six man body made up of three Canadians and three Americans. I believe the staff of the Canadian section includes one engineer only, one lawyer. It looks to government personnel in each country to find answers, factual answers and make technical judgments. These studies are provided by agencies of the Canadian government, of the U.S. government and, on occasion, provincial and state water resources commissions.
Our technical people in the new department of environment, with the people from the Ontario Water Resources Commission in the case of the lower lakes, will be doing all of the basic technical analyses. We will be
Government Organization Act, 1970 making many of the technical recommendations that flow up to the International Joint Commission. Those six gentlemen, in their wisdom, will make certain general recommendations to the heads of government in the two nations. So, coming back to the same technical people, these recommendations will, in large measure, stem from their technical expertise in the first place, and will be coming back to them to enforce. Of course, the IJC, in its wisdom will make the recommendations, delete some, and perhaps modify others, but the technical overlap is at an absolute minimum. There is no duplication and the technical recommendations made by our staff to this IJC may be recommendations which they, months later, will be required to enforce.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the minister's statement that under the new regulations the federal government insisted that Manitoba Hydro take steps to assure the water flow in the Nelson River, behind the dams that are being built, would be sufficient to protect the ecology in that area. Could he tell us what he and his department are doing about the pollution of very important waters in the province of Manitoba by industries outside the province?
Lake Winnipeg is one of the largest lakes in the country, and probably for a hundred years very important commercial fishing operations have been conducted there. Now, the lake has been closed to commercial fishing because it has been polluted. The Manitoba government is in the process of taking legal action against a paper company in Dryden, Ontario, and against a chemical company in Saskatoon which has been discharging poisonous material into the Saskatchewan River which flows into Lake Winnipeg. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, you have been following the line of questioning quite closely for the last half hour or three quarters of an hour. I am sure you will agree that all members are faced with a dilemma in view of the scope of this bill. Clause 4 reads:
The Governor in Council may appoint an officer called the Deputy Minister of the Environment to be the deputy head of the Department of the Environment and to hold office during pleasure.
As I stated when speaking during the debate on second reading, I have no objection to establishing a department of the environment with a deputy minister of the environment whose prime responsibilities will be related to pollution control, especially as it affects our seacoast and inland fisheries. The department will also be responsible for our renewable resources, including the forest resources of Canada, migratory birds and other domestic flora and fauna. The department will be responsible for meteorology reports, the protection and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment, including water, air and soil quality. It will be responsible for technical surveys within the meaning of the Resources and Technical Surveys Act as well as the enforcement of any rules
February 4, 1971

or regulations made by the International Joint Commission which may be promulgated pursuant to the treaty between the United States of America and His Majesty King Edward VII relating to boundary waters and questions arising between the United States and Canada as far as they relate to pollution control.
I feel sure that all members will agree this is a tall order. The minister and the deputy minister, who will be responsible for the administration of this department, will be kept more than busy. In view of the many and varied responsibilities heaped upon the minister and the deputy minister by the establishment of this new department of the environment, all members from Atlantic Canada are concerned that the department of fisheries, which is being phased out by this legislation, will become the unwanted stepchild of this new department. This will, of course, be unfortunate, especially in view of the importance of this industry to many important areas of Atlantic Canada where fishing is a way of life, and where the income derived from fishing is the only income available in some regions of economic disparity.
Fishing provides a livelihood for some 68,000 Canadian fishermen and it is estimated that the value of fishery products derived from last year's catch, of which 70 per cent was exported, will amount to approximately $370 million. However, part of this industry is today being threatened by mercury pollution of the seas. Only last week some 30,000 pounds of swordfish landed in Nova Scotia were found to contain mercury to the extent that they were unsaleable for human consumption. This has resulted in the closing down of this industry. In reply to a question I put to the present Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, as reported on page 2941 of Hansard, the minister replied:
Unfortunately, most swordfish caught on the high seas at a considerable distance from Canada contain more than the half part per million of mercury.
He then went on to say that the government would endeavour to do much the same thing as was done for other fisheries in this country, namely, support the incomes of fishermen until they can find work in another segment of the fishery or be retrained for employment in other industries. Mr. Chairman, this is not good enough. Many of our fishermen do not wish to leave a way of life or a vocation which they have followed since childhood. Some are incapable of learning another trade, while others have a lifetime of earnings and savings invested in ships and fishing gear which today cannot be used as a mean of providing for their needs and the needs of their wives and families. I ask the minister and I ask the government: what are these men to do with their ships and with their fishing equipment? Even if they qualify for retraining, who is to pay them for their equipment now made obsolete by the pollution of the seas?
It seems to me that the government has an immediate and urgent responsibility to determine the source of mercury pollution in some species of fish, especially swordfish and tuna. Fortunately, we have a large oceanographic base at Bedford Basin near Halifax, and one of our
Government Organization Act, 1970
first priorities should be to undertake an immediate water study in the hope of determining the sources of mercury pollution. As the matter is also of concern to the United States, I feel certain that the American government would be willing, if approached, to co-operate by making its facilities at Woods Hole, Massachusetts, available for a joint water study.
I mention these matters in connection with the clause under review because I wish to make it clear that the deputy minister of the environment will bear vast and varied responsibilities. I have given the committee an outline of some of them, and there are one or two other items I wish to bring to the attention of the committee in order to buttress the motion I intend to move at the conclusion of my remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. As I say, I intend to move an amendment at the conclusion of my remarks.
I referred to the fact that this question might well be of concern to the United States government. As it happens, it is the regulations enforced in the United States which prevent our selling swordfish to that country. I believe 90 per cent of the catch goes to that market. This is something the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry should be doing. He should be working quickly in consultation with the United States to determine the sources of mercury pollution.
It may well be that mercury compounds in anti-fouling paints used on the bottoms of our ships are among the culprits or it may be the methods used in the manufacture of caustic soda by shore installations are adding greater quantities of mercury to our air and water than first realized. I cannot help but wonder if the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry has given any thought to outlawing the present method of producing caustic soda which releases mercury tainted waste. There is another method which might be used but it is more expensive, and industry resists making a costly change-over.
Can anything be done to prevent an increase of these plants? Last spring, when the Lake St. Clair fisheries were closed, there was a great deal of publicity about mercury pollution. One newspaper article mentioned that there were a dozen chlor-alkali plants releasing mercury across Canada, including one shortly to go into operation in Nova Scotia.
Now, in Ontario, they have found that reducing the amount of mercury entering the water has no effect on reducing the mercury level already present. In other words, mercury does not dissipate as does radio-activity. Once it is there, it is there to stay. Notwithstanding this, in the Globe and Mail of January 19, 1971, we read:
Dow Chemical of Canada Limited is still dumping mercury from the Sarnia plant into the St. Clair River and the governments of Canada and Ontario are considering legal action, the U.S. Supreme Court was told yesterday.
This company has now located in Nova Scotia, and I wonder if the process they will use in their chlor-alkali plant will add more mercury to our sea water. Has the
February 4, 1971

Government Organization Act, 1970 minister investigated this company's plans, and were they approved by his department?

speechtext:
That you, Mr. Chairman, but if you will bear with me I am sure you will see my point. As it is at present, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry and his deputy minister are more than overloaded with responsibilities pertaining to fisheries alone. Clause 4 provides only for the appointment of one deputy minister of the environment. Obviously, if the existing deputy minister is, along with his minister, unable to cope adequately with the problems facing the department, the arrangements we are now asked to make are not adequate. I want to lay the background in support of an argument for a special, separate deputy minister for the fisheries to ensure that the fisheries, along the problems of Canadian fishermen, do not become orphans. These are not problems which can be taken lightly. These are projects we must carry out immediately. The whole chain of our fisheries resources might be threatened if there is delay.
For these reasons and many others I could cite, I firmly believe we should have a separate deputy minister of fisheries. He would be responsible for the continued good health of our fishing industry and would not only look into matters such as mercury pollution but lead the fight for the preservation of the fishing resources on our continental shelf, which today are seriously threatened by overfishing from massive fleets of foreign nations.
The proposed deputy minister of environment has a good reputation for competence arising out of his success as deputy commissioner general of Expo '67. But a resume of his previous activities makes absolutely no reference to any experience in matters relating to fisheries. This lack of fishing knowledge will not be helpful to our industry or to Canada when we meet with other fishing nations for discussion of our fisheries resources at the next Law of the Sea Conference to be held in 1972. Who will press for a solution to the thorny problems concerning relations between France and Canada as they relate to fishing rights surrounding the French-owned islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon? Since 1964 we have been told these matters are under discussion with the French government, but we have never received a report in this House on the result of those discussions. While this question of fishing rights around these islands is unresolved, we can never fully implement our 1964 Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act-our 12-mile limit legislation.
For these reasons, and for many more that I could mention, I want to move the following amendment. One of my colleagues has just asked me what I mean by "these reasons", and I am referring to the reasons I have given, though there are others. The deputy minister of the department of the environment will have conflicting

responsibilities. On the one hand, he will be responsible for the purity of our water and our air while, on the other hand, he will be responsible for the development of our renewable resources. However, sometimes the development of our resources brings with it the polluton of our water and our air, so I am just wondering which hat the deputy minister of the environment will be wearing when he is faced with this problem.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate:
That clause 4 of Bill C-207 be amended by adding thereto, next after line 3 on page 2 thereof, the following:
"(2) Notwithstanding subsection (1) the Governor in Council may appoint an officer called the Deputy Minister of Fisheries to hold office during pleasure and to perform all such duties and functions of a deputy head as extend to and include all matters relating to sea coast and inland fisheries."

Just going back over the last two decades we find that a number of nations, including not only coastal states but some of the eastern European nations that are not coastal states, have developed their fisheries to such an extent that Canada's fishing efforts appear miniscule in comparison. For example, two decades ago Russia was almost unheard of as a fishing nation. Countries like West Germany, Poland, Roumania, the Scandinavian countries and the countries in southwest Europe have continued making major efforts to become fishing nations.
The minister of fisheries knows that the marine environment as a renewable resource-I am not referring to mineral resources or to oil, which are non-renewable resources-is one of the great frontiers of Canada, yet in many ways is unexplored and undeveloped. Bill C-207 now before the committee seeks to eliminate the fisheries department. My colleague from South Shore has placed on the record in no uncertain terms the contradiction implied in the government's move to create numerous ministers of state and, on the other hand, to eliminate entirely the department of fisheries. speechtext:
On a more serious note, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the amendment which has been proposed to the committee by the hon. member for South Shore may be the answer to the conundrum with which a number of us in this House have been wrestling ever since it became apparent that the proposal for the establishment of the department of environment would involve the merging into that department of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. Those of us who participated in the discussions last session on the amendments to the Fisheries Act had it impressed upon us very firmly, as a result of evidence and debate, that undoubtedly the Fisheries Act stood in the front line of the defence of water quality across Canada. So, I think there is undoubtedly much virtue in the idea of establishing a department where policies in respect of water quality and fisheries are co-ordinated. It is apparent that this is part and parcel of the proposal in this part of the bill which involves the setting up of a department of environment.
The question that has very obviously been of concern to some members from the Atlantic coast who represent many commercial fishermen, and some of us from the Pacific coast who also represent areas where the commercial fisheries are very important, is the apparent dissolution of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, or what might be construed as a downgrading of it. I think many commercial fishermen have, quite rightly, been fearful that in the process of setting up this new department with much broader responsibilities under the minis-
Government Organization Act, 1970 ter who has been the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, less attention, less money and less effort will be given to the commercial fisheries. So, I think the proposal put forward by the hon. member for South Shore may be in part at least, the answer to the problem.
As I understand the functioning of a department, the primary responsibility at the policy level rests with the minister who, together with his colleagues in the cabinet makes determinations of policy directions. I would agree that in the areas which are under discussion, particularly those relating to fisheries and water-leaving aside for a moment the sections of the bill which deal with air and soil quality-close co-ordination at the policy level by a minister who is prepared to evolve a policy for the protection of the over-all environment, can very well be tied in with creating the necessary circumstances for the growth and survival of fish. However, if my understanding is correct, the main function of the deputy head of a department is that of administration. I would be prepared to argue that the administration of a department involved with the commercial fisheries is certainly important enough to warrant the full time of a deputy minister.
Our present department is called the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, and we had no quarrel with the concept of adding to the department of fisheries the federal responsibility in the area of forestry. I think members of the committee will recognize when we are talking about fisheries and forestry we are really talking about-I was going to say-two different kettles of fish so far as the operations of the federal government are concerned. As has often been said, the primary jurisdiction constitutionally over forestry and forestry resources of Canada, their harvesting and development, rests with the provincial governments. However with regard to fisheries federal jurisdiction over seacoast and inland fisheries is firmly embedded in the BNA Act. So, in this particular area we exercise a jurisdiction over the management and the well-being of this resource industry that is parallel to the powers exercised by the provinces in relation to forestry.
Essentially, what happened was that we played an ancillary role in respect of the forest industry in Canada by undertaking research programs, and programs leading towards fire protection, protection from disease and that sort of thing. In addition, of course, the federal government agreed to co-operate with the provinces in the development of an inventory. But, Mr. Chairman, those are very different kinds of responsibilities administratively than administering the very far flung commercial fisheries of Canada which involve three oceans in addition to the vast inland waters that we have in this country. So, I think a very logical argument can be developed for the proposition that, even if we were having a unified ministry, there should be two deputy heads.
The hon. member who preceded me made some reference to the apparent lack of interest of the Department of External Affairs in fishing matters. I am not sure I

February 4, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
agree with all of his observations in detail, but for a period of years I have felt that our Department of External Affairs regards the increasingly important international questions involved in the survival of our commercial fisheries as very peripheral matters so far as the foreign policy of Canada is concerned. This may perhaps be another good reason why we should have at least a deputy minister of fisheries who, from time to time, can deal as a co-equal with his opposite number in the Department of External Affairs. I think even the unmarinated Secretary of State for External Affairs would agree that there is a need for very close co-operation on the matter of fisheries. I hope he will more and more agree that his department should be a very important arm of what, up to now, has been called our department of fisheries if we are to maintain this resource, and if it is going to be worth while putting federal money into helping develop this resource.
I would like to point out to the committee that this proposition of having two deputy heads within a single department is not an unprecedented proposal. In fact, at the present time we have two deputy heads within the Department of National Health and Welfare, one with responsibility for the administration of health matters and the other with responsibility for welfare matters. Over a period of a great many years in the Department of National Revenue there were two deputy heads, a deputy minister for customs and excise, and a deputy minister of taxation, performing pretty well defined functions but under the general policy jurisdiction of a single minister. I have not heard that this created any insuperable problems in that department.
So, I suggest that this proposal which has been placed before us has merit. Certainly, it is worthy of very serious consideration. Undoubtedly, there will be overlapping of areas of responsibility in some respects. Such bodies, for example, as the Fisheries Research Board undoubtedly would be providing expertise which would flow through both the deputy head of the environment and the deputy head of fisheries. Nevertheless, as I see it, the responsibility of the minister for the commercial fisheries of Canada is pretty clear, distinct and well defined, and necessitates a full-time deputy head.
As has been so often stated, there has been argument among fishermen, and even in this House, that we really need two ministers of fisheries, one for the Atlantic coast and one for the Pacific coast. I have never accepted that proposition. When it has been suggested to me by fishermen on the west coast, I have tried to point out that it could lead to differences in policy matters and I do not think we want this. But undoubtedly there is a need for differences in administration regionally as between the Atlantic coast and the Pacific coast, and there is also a need for co-ordination of administraton, which of course must take place at the headquarters of a department.
So, Mr. Chairman, I would ask hon. members of the committee, including those who occupy positions on the treasury benches, to give serious consideration to the amendment that has been proposed. I think it may go a long way toward satisfying the real and legitimate concern that commercial fishermen across Canada will have
at the apparent disappearance of fisheries as a separate ministry within the operations of the federal government.

I think that when we talk about the war on poverty we must know what the government is attempting to do. It ought to tell members of the House what its plans are for dealing with this situation. In my opinion, it is not good enough for those plans to be used for the internal purposes of the department only. If members of the House are to debate intelligently the proposed actions of the government, they ought to have access to that information obtained as a result of research by experts. That information is available to the government and to the department concerned, but has not been given to the House of Commons. Even though the information may be in a form that is suitable only for internal use, as is the case here, I think that the government ought to make such information available to the members of this House in an abbreviated form. Perhaps the information could be provided in such a way as to enable hon. members to know where the government is going.
Unfortunately, it appears that the government is using the war on poverty as an excuse for saying that this information cannot be divulged. We know that poverty is no longer merely of domestic concern. It is a national disgrace. Every member of the House, I submit, thinks that something must be done to cure poverty, and the research undertaken in this area, research going back over the years, ought to be made available to the House in order that hon. members may have a concrete idea of what is being done to eradicate poverty. The House of Commons and the people of this country are under an obligation to eradicate poverty in this country.
We know that once poverty takes root in a certain area or in a certain group, it completely destroys the fibre of that part of our society. If unchecked, it will destroy the fibre of our society and of our nation in the long run. I need not cite examples of poverty in any particular area of the country but we know that once grinding poverty sets in, hopeless despair is the result. As a result of that despair, the people affected by poverty will act; they will try to destroy that which brought about their poverty. I hope that we can prevent, in future, the sort of destruction we have witnessed in the past. The government and society must act to prevent this type of destruction. We can only prevent it if we are serious about fighting the war on poverty and if we consider the problem of poverty in its entirety.
Some are aware, I am sure, that the people of the middle classes would like to close their eyes to the war on poverty. They consider that policies such as urban renewal are sufficient for dealing with poverty. Our middle classes think as "haves" and they would like to think they are unaffected by the real problems of the "have nots". While this attitude persists, I submit that it will take a long time to bring about any changes in the conditions of the poor in our society. If we are to fight the war against poverty effectively, we must revolutionize our thinking in connection with such matters as pollution and unemployment, as well as many others which have been mentioned in the House of Commons. In this country we must bring about an employment ratio that will permit us to do away with poverty. We must be able

They are not trained for any particular occupations to be found in large urban centres, and there are no jobs for them. Clearly, we ought to be concerned about the rural poor. Our present system, under which we move the rural poor to our cities, will create difficulties that are graver than this government may realize. It appears that-there is a concentrated effort to put more farmland into the hands of large corporations and a result, there will be less and less employment on the land.
We know very well that many people in the country have voiced a wish to bring about some type of change. May I refer to what the Canadian Welfare Council has said? Mr. Reuben C. Baetz, executive director of the Council, has said the following:
If the just society is ever going to be anything more than a meaningless and flimsy abstraction, it must be based on certain tangible, fundamental rights, including social as well as civil and political rights. Mr. Chairman, the amendment to clause 4 which we are now discussing deals with the appointment of a deputy minister in charge of fisheries. As was pointed out by the hon. member for South Shore, the reason for the amendment is very simple, namely, we feel that the new department of the environment will be taking over the responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries plus new, added responsibilities. That is why we proposed this amendment and that is why we support it. It is essential that the Department of Fisheries be maintained as a definite entity within the new department.
I contend, as I have before-I do not intend to speak too long on this matter-that the minister will have more than he can handle as minister of the environment. This is why we from the Atlantic provinces proposed the amendment. We want to make sure that the problems of the fishermen will receive attention. The minister knows that I applauded him whenever he introduced programs that were worth-while to fishermen, and that I was critical of him when he introduced programs that I thought were detrimental to the interests of fishermen, or that at least were not in accordance with my ideas. Therefore, he knows that it is not out of criticism of him that I support this amendment.
We know that the minister is from the west coast and that he is very much interested in pollution matters. Having been in charge of fisheries and forestry for the past 2i years, he is probably looking for a new challenge; therefore, I suspect he will be paying a lot more attention to environmental matters than to fisheries. Let there be no mistake, Mr. Chairman: none of us is opposed to the establishment of a department of the environment, but we believe there should be a deputy minister responsible for fisheries as well as a deputy minister responsible for forestry and for pollution in general. Therefore, I say the amendment is a valid one. Its validity is not in question at the moment; it has been accepted and we are debating it. We know that the minister and his parliamentary secretary will want to accept this amendment. His parliamentary secretary shakes his head in disagreement.
[The Acting Chairman (Mr. Richard).]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES ETC.
speechtext: I have confidence in the minister.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES ETC.
speechtext:
So have I; but I want to make sure that a Deputy Minister of Fisheries will be appointed, and if I dared to go further than the terms of the amendment I would ask that he be from the east coast. Although the parliamentary secretary comes from the east coast, he does not represent a real fishing area. Therefore I say the proposed deputy minister should come from the Atlantic region.
The minister will have added responsibilities in the new department. Many problems connected with the fisheries remain unanswered and I do not believe they will receive full attention when the new department is established. The minister and the parliamentary secretary may argue that the appointment of another parliamentary secretary responsible for fisheries would help, and that they will have a parliamentary secretary in charge of fisheries and a parliamentary secretary responsible for environmental affairs. I do not consider that adequate.
As I have said, there are many fisheries problems that have not yet been solved. There are problems in connection with the 12-mile limit. Not long before Christmas the minister ordered the closing of certain bays to foreign fishermen, including the Bay of Fundy, the Gulf of St. Lawrence and certain bays on the coast of British Columbia. But that is not sufficient, Mr. Chairman; it does not fully meet the interests of the fishermen. This closure does not include one of the great herring spawning areas of the Atlantic region around Trinity Ledge; it is not protected from foreign fishermen.
This morning's newspapers record another complaint concernings the lobster season. Some of the fishermen are not satisfied. They have made dozens of representations with respect to the lobster season, particularly in District 4. A deputy minister in charge of fisheries would be able to pay more attention to such things than a general deputy minister in charge of many matters. There is another problem connected with the fisheries that has not been fully solved and which is becoming more serious as time passes. Last May the minister announced a program of assistance for the construction of fishing boats but to date the regulations affecting boats of 75-feet and over have not been promulgated. I know that they have to be made in co-operation with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, but the delay is becoming longer and longer.
If the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Shore is accepted, a deputy minister of fisheries would be able to tackle some of these problems. I know the minister is a good listener, as is his parliamentary secretary. I know that when they have heard all the arguments they will wish to accept the amendment. I repeat that fisheries must remain an entity within the new department and that there is a relationship between fisheries and the environment. Recently a question was raised concerning both. The Department of Fisheries has banned swordfishing on the east coast because of mercury pollution, and the fishermen involved will have to engage in some other activity at least for a while. I ask, what is to be done for them? It is a very important fishery on the Atlantic coast and also on the west coast.
February 4, 1971

These fishermen will have to devote their energies to other ventures. The Department of Fisheries ought to suggest what the fishermen should do next.
Unquestionably, mercury pollution affects our environment; there is no question about that. Nevertheless, these fishermen must enter another field of the fishery. They can only do that if their interests are taken into account. Someone in the Department of Fisheries must say to these people, "You can fish for scallops or go into another field, but there are limitations in certain areas." For those reasons there must be a deputy minister in charge of fisheries. As I say, there are too many questions still unanswered. Once the new department is set up and once the minister is given these added responsibilities, it is less likely that we shall obtain the answers to some of our questions. The Department of Fisheries is much too important merely to be amalgamated into the conglomeration which is being set up. The minister is to take over some of the responsibilities of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and, in addition, some of the responsibilities of other departments. Therefore, too much will be left to one deputy minister who must also deal with fisheries. I submit, therefore, that a deputy minister in charge of fisheries should be appointed.
The minister is most enthusiastic about pollution control. I expect almost everyone here is enthusiastic about pollution control. At the same time, a proper balance must be struck and we must consider the interests of our fisheries. I said that many problems have been left unanswered. I was referring to fisheries regulations, to matters such as the lobster season and the 12-mile limit. There is also a problem with regard to fishermen who catch swordfish. Are they to engage in another part of the fishery? What is to become of these fishermen? I hope the minister will make a statement shortly about the mercury content of swordfish, for example. 1 hope his statement will be to the effect that the consumer need not be scared and that all fish are not contaminated. I know he has already said something along these lines.
What would happen if the consumer who will not eat swordfish suddenly were to say, "I am not going to eat scallops or lobster either"? That situation must be avoided and the minister must make a positive statement to allay fears. I am sure he will do that in due course. Many problems have not yet been solved in this field. With the additional responsibilities the minister is to assume, they will receive less attention. For that reason I say this amendment is a good one and should be accepted.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak briefly on the amendment before the House. I speak in support of the amendment. I submit that the amendment is simple yet it is essential. I do not understand why the government should not accept the idea that since we are now setting up a new department of the environment which will encompass the Department of Fisheries and Forestry and, in addition, assume responsibilities in the field of the environment, there should be appointed two deputy ministers each of whom should have clear and distinct
Government Organization Act, 1970 duties. That is what the amendment seeks to do and I think it is an excellent idea.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it is plain common sense to remember that if you are going to enlarge the activities of a department and one man is to be given responsibility for the enlarged department, he will be able to give less time to the fisheries and forestry responsibilities of the department. I think we are making a mistake in not keeping the responsibilities relating to the environment clear and separate from all other responsibilities of the department. If that is not done, we shall find ourselves in a position we have been in so often. We will find, on the one hand, that the deputy minister of the department will be in charge of fisheries and forestry, resources which are exploited, and economic interests will be involved; but on the other hand we will find that the same minister must sit down and try to talk out of both sides of his mouth. Out of one side of his mouth he will say, "We will do this." Then from the other side of his mouth he will say, "No, nothing doing. We must hold the reins in because what is proposed will affect the environment; therefore, we shall have to clamp down on the type of development proposed." That would not make any sense.

speechtext: There would be a conflict of interest.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES ETC.
speechtext:
There would be a clear conflict of interest and without doubt we would get into trouble if the department were set up that way. Since we are setting up this department now, let us do it properly: let us have two deputy ministers. Other departments of government have two deputy ministers. In the Department of National Health and Welfare a deputy minister is in charge of one part of the department and another deputy minister is in charge of another part. All we are asking is that one deputy minister be appointed to be responsible for fisheries and forestry and that another be appointed to take charge of the environmental responsibilities of the department. To me, that makes sense.
May I point out again that once you create a conflict of interest you will not be able to do the sort of job that ought to be done with respect to the fisheries responsibilities of the department or with respect to the environmental responsibilities. I think that is clear. The Science Council of Canada in its last report indicated to the government what ought to be done so far as fisheries are concerned. That body asked for a vast increase in the number of research projects on the east coast, the west coast and inland waters. It told the government that we need to have at our disposal vastly increased information in certain fields.
Also, the Science Council told the government that we are not assessing to the full the potential of our fisheries in all parts of the nation. This indicates to me, Mr. Chairman, that the fisheries responsibilities of the department ought to be expanded, especially so far as research and allied activities are concerned. It seems to me, however, that we are to load the responsibilities of a brand new department on top of the responsibilities of the existing department, and therefore we shall not obtain satisfactory results in all areas.

I will not go into all the details which have been covered by previous speakers. I reiterate that this is a sound and sensible amendment. I hope that this Liberal government for once in its life will accept one of the recommendations of the opposition and appoint two deputy ministers of the department. That would increase the department's efficiency; it would be good for Canada and good for both the fisheries and the environmental branches of the department. We need this deputy minister, so let us adopt the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make on the amendment of the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) to Clause 4 of Bill C-207 which provides for the appointment of a second deputy minister who would be exclusively responsible for fishery legislation.
In Schedule A of Bill C-207, we note there are 19 acts relating to fisheries, 16 of which directly concern water utilization and fisheries.
Mr. Chairman, at first sight it would seem that the area of fisheries has been neglected in the new department of environment. However, those 16 acts on fisheries already exist and there is also a Department of Fisheries and Forestry that is responsible for their administration.
I greatly hesitate to support the amendment of the member for South Shore, because it tends to multiply more and more important positions in the government administration. It often happens that deputy ministers have more authority than ministers themselves. In the first place, they receive a higher salary and they seem to have better control over the officials around them than ministers do.
Mr. Chairman, the members and a large segment of the population-especially fishermen-are concerned by the result of the report which has just been communicated to us and according to which tuna and swordfish fishing is greatly compromised due to the mercury pollution of sea-water.
Nothing prevents the Canadian government from asking American authorities to fight mercury pollution. However, it has occurred. With a deputy minister directly responsible for the enforcement of fishery legislation, I wonder whether there would be an increase in efficiency.
Even if the bill does not provide for the appointment of a second deputy minister who would be responsible for the enforcement of fishery legislation, the minister still has the authority needed to appoint all the officials required to handle environmental affairs and water pollution matters. These officials will look after the implementation of fishery legislation designed to protect not just the fishermen from the Maritimes but also the fishermen from British Columbia and the Canadian consumers.
Although we five in central Canada, we are very concerned by the Canadian fishermen's activities because we are aware that if they cannot sail for the high seas to catch the swordfish, this will be reflected in higher consumer prices not only for swordfish, but also for other species of fish and sea products.
I am not at all sure that it will be necessary to appoint a second deputy minister to the Department of the Environment. I believe that we should rather give the present minister more power over his officials and provide the latter with the required freedom to wage war against pollution and implement the existing laws.

I do not particularly want to invite Your Honour at Christmas; it would be better to visit in the spring, summer or fall when the countryside is delightful.
I wish to make a few comments in support of the amendment now before us. I do not represent a large segment of the fishing community but I do represent a typical and very significant part of the total fishing industry on the Atlantic coast. There are hundreds of full-time inshore or groundfishermen. The families of fishermen I represent have fished for generations. Their fathers and grandfathers were fishermen as well as their sons and grandsons. They have all fished off the eastern shore of Nova Scotia. These people have pride in their way of life and ability to provide for their families. These things cannot be dealt with lightly. Their support of this traditional way of life has been characteristic of the support that has built Canada in a maritime sense.
The fact that this bill will deprive them of the right to recognition within the bounds of ministerial or governmental prerogative is not important. What is important is that if they are deprived of the identification of their way of life, this will be very harmful. I could speak meaningfully about fishermen from Ecum Secum to Halifax and from Halifax to Hubbards. However, this has already been eminently done by the hon. member for South Western Nova and the mover of this amendment. I support their views and concern. I simply echo the concern of those who live in Dartmouth and along the eastern shore of Nova Scotia.
What I wanted to do, because it is appropriate to the bill albeit a little out of context but still very important with respect to the development of this new department

of the environment, was talk to the minister for a moment or two about the way in which he ought to approach the question of information about his department. If I go a little outside the scope of the amendment I can quickly bring myself back within its terms, Mr. Chairman, and I know you will remind me if necessary. In recent months we have heard a good deal about information arrangements. I relate this in no small way to the role of information regarding the omnibus bill which is before us, because it is important in that sense if not in the total sense. Perhaps before we vote on the amendment tonight and move to the next clause, the minister will express his views on the subject and answer some questions I have in mind.
I wonder whether with respect to information the minister has considered instituting his own system. Will the new department have its own resources in dollars and cents and professional expertise to build up its own data system, experts who will be able to identify, through his policy directions, his needs in terms of the acceptability to the department of the environment of information from other sources? Or will he develop his own source in response to the need for bringing to him the type of information which would satisfy his requirements? I wonder if he intends to do anything about the storage of such data. I wonder if he will do anything about retrieving it as required. I wonder what he intends to do about computerizing it. I wonder what he intends to do about analysing it.

speechtext:
I am talking about a deputy minister, the man through whom the minister must translate into practical working arrangements his own particular views. I can do this in half an hour or it can be done now, but one way or another you will get a little lecture from the junior member for Halifax about careful planning. I will bring it within the scope of the debate by indicating the necessity for a deputy minister. I do not think it is in character for the minister to be smart or impertinent. He has had a bad week or ten days. What hon. members opposite do not need in this chamber tonight, what the minister does not need, are enemies, particularly as he goes ahead with the work in front of him.
I wonder how he would go about creating the type of staff which will analyse this information, in the sense that it will be useful to him and to the people who are directly affected, in this case the fisheries; but not only fisheries, the total environmental program. The opportunity to say a few words on fisheries when there are so many members in the House is rare, because I have never seen more than a dozen hon. members in the House when we have been talking about fisheries. I would like to supplement the remarks of my colleague, the outstanding fishermen's representative from South Shore who has been involved in fisheries ever since he was knee-high to a grasshopper, a man who understands the fishing industry of Canada from the dory to the dragger, the long-liner and the like. I was amazed a few minutes ago to hear several hon. members ask, "What the heck is a long-liner?" Someone else asked, "What is groundfish?" Perhaps they think it is something you put through a mincer to end up as a patty. I am not surprised at this lack of knowledge about fisheries in the House of Commons because we do not often have fish on the menu here.
We have in Canada five provinces on the Atlantic coast and one on the Pacific coast which are directly affected by the fishing industry. There is British Columbia, the east part of Quebec, the Gaspe area and the four Atlantic provinces. I do not know whether members know this, but fishing was the staple industry of the nation. They did not start Canada with the great industrial complexes of Ontario. They did not develop the railway across Canada to open up the fishing industry, either. That came a lot later than 1497. People came over from Europe and asked why we did not turn the east coast of Canada into a marvellous garden of marine resources, a great area where there exists the most advanced marine resource industry in the world.
The British, 400 years ago, milked the economy of the Atlantic region with their great naval fleets. The Spaniards sent out their fleets and so did the Portugese. They came across the Atlantic and developed the economy of the Atlantic region which supplemented their own economies. That was the beginning of these great European nations. The British always treated Newfoundland as a vessel moored off the Gulf of St. Lawrence, a very convenient vessel moored along great fishing banks such as the Grand Banks, the Georgia Banks and all the great fishing areas of the Labrador coast, Hamilton Inlet and Groswater Bay. We could never really develop our fishing industry because of lack of industrial expansion and because we did not have the type of taxation base to give us the necessary funds.
