I am not at all surprised that the Chair does not recognize the relevancy of my argument. In 1968, for example, the Russians took 25 per cent of the fish stock off the Hamilton Inlet Banks, which are the great spawning grounds for the Labrador fishery. The amount of fish they took was one billion pounds, enough to keep the biggest fish plant in my riding going for 100 years.
Canada has sat on its haunches. It has not moved aggressively to protect these resources. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has not had the backbone, the courage or perhaps the interest to take any initiative. We have not identified this industry as being important enough. We have not been determined to harvest these resources ourselves. Mr. Chairman, just check the tins of kippers that you put on hors d'oeuvre at your cocktail parties and you will find they do not come from Nova Scotia, P.E.I. or Newfoundland. They come from Europe, because the Germans sent over great fleets to take the herring, package them and send them back to us.
The Norwegians and the Icelanders have developed their fishing resources. The fisheries are almost their
Government Organization Act, 1970 whole economy. But what have we done? This year, after all the fuss we have had about fish, all the racket we have raised, the "W5" programs on television with the minister coming across on the tube and saying he is aware of the problem, with the people of B.C. almost launching a naval attack on the Russians, and after the bilateral discussions we have had with the Russians, what have we done? We are going to retire the Deputy Minister of Fisheries. We are going to get rid of the Department of Fisheries. After spending a lifetime in the service of the fisheries, we are going to retire Dr. Needier and tell him, "If we want your advice one of these days, we will ask you."
The Minister of Fisheries is not concerned. He is moving into an area in which he is very competent. I know he will be competent in controlling various types of pollution. This is the job he has been seeking. But the government has not said that it will appoint one of the proposed ministers of state to be responsible for fisheries. No longer will we be able to ask questions in the House of the Minister of Fisheries. Instead, we will have a minister of the environment, another man called the deputy minister of the environment, and away down the line we will have an assistant, an associate, a kind of director or some other kind of character responsible for fisheries. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 13, as reported at page 2369 of Hansard, I
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board the following question:
In view of representations by representatives of the farm organizations concerning the storage of the six major grains, can the minister say whether or not the government has decided to share the cost of storage of some basic amount of these six major grains, or whether the government is at least considering such a policy?
The minister replied that discussions were going on with the producers about many things-I did not ask him about many things-but that it was not his intention to speculate on the results of the discussions until a full announcement could be made. I chose to discuss the matter on this occasion because I hope that the minister will reconsider what seems to me to be a position on which he has already made up his mind. It seems to me that the minister gave me a non-answer, one that many in the House, and more importantly the members of farm organizations, feel indicates conclusively not only that the government is going to cancel its program of sharing with the producers the storage costs of wheat but that his mind is closed on this and other similar measures.
With this type of stubbornness and arrogance the minister continues to ignore basic principles and minimal fundamentals that apply to agriculture, specifically-in this case-to western grain farmers. He offers not the slightest acknowledgement or even shows an awareness of the fact that, in fairness if nothing else, the Prairie grain farmer is entitled to treatment and benefits that are at least equal to those the government feels justified in providing to other sectors of the economy, sectors that are not nearly so basic to our economy.
The government to which the minister belongs feels it is fair and proper to pay up to $120 million to store and stockpile uranium, to pay millions of dollars to support our gold mines or to pay millions to subsidize the railroads, but that somehow it is bad for the nation to share with the Prairie grain farmers the cost of storing a reasonable inventory of grain. In his proposal-and had the minister proposed in this way to a lady he would have been a born loser-the minister states that the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act would be abolished. This is an item that has cost the federal government an average of $41 million a year since 1956. By abolishing this measure the minister-I suspect in agreement with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), if not at his urging- will then have funds to pay most, if not all, of what he might need to put into what he calls the grain income stabilization fund.
This means that little or no new federal money will go into the western grain industry, particularly after the current crop year. In other words, the minister can be a hero to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance by using money already provided for a different purpose, getting the federal government off the hook so far as participating to a greater extent in the assistance of western agriculture is concerned. The Temporary Wheat Reserves Act gave proper recognition to the principle that the country as a whole has a responsi-

February 4, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion bility to bear a fair share of storing an inventory of wheat, as is the case with gold. That act is not perfect; I think the minister as well as I would agree that there are inadequacies in it. But at least it took account of the benefit to the nation as a whole of maintaining an inventory of "on ship" or "en route to on ship" loading of western wheat.
Public responsibility for sharing the cost of storing this grain recognized the benefits to the nation as a whole of grain exports, as well as what it does for our foreign exchange position, for enabling our importers to have new avenues of trade with other nations and for the nation in the eyes of other countries, particularly those who buy our wheat. The minister can choose not to consider my views or those of my colleagues and I would not blame him for that. After all, we are members of the New Democratic Party and he is a Liberal. I can understand that, accept it and even forgive him for it. But he ignores at his peril and at the peril of agriculture the spokesmen of those organizations which represent farmers. This is due in no small measure to the fact that you will not find stronger advocates for the case of justice for the grain farmer than you find today in the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and other Liberal members from the Prairies who have been supporting the farmers so stongly.
The hon. member asks about farm representation. I say to him that when I put to farm organizations the question whether they are simply asking that more money be paid or whether they really want a storage program, they admit each and every one that it is the former rather than the latter in which they are interested. If the Wheat Board, for instance, were to pay for on-farm storage, and therefore the final price to the farmer would be lower, they would no longer be interested in such a program.
This simply turns us back once again to the fundamental and broad argument about whether it is right for the
treasury to pay for the support of the grain industry. As I think our proposal indicates, our commitment in this regard has and is increasing, due in large measure to the stalwart support for the grain farmer of the Liberal members in this House.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-INQUIRY AS TO CONTINUATION OF FEED GRAIN FREIGHT ASSISTANCE
AGRICULTURE-INQUIRY AS TO CONTINUATION OF FEED GRAIN FREIGHT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, as recorded at page 2892 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) the following question:
Could the hon. gentlemen indicate whether feed grain freight assistance will be continued, as requested at the meeting this week of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture?
The minister replied:
-early last summer we indicated that the rates in effect now will continue until the end of this fiscal year. Of course, in the new fiscal year we will have to bring estimates before the House for the appropriation of funds for the levels we set for that year.
I then asked:
I wonder whether the minister would tell me whether he said yes to me or whether he said no.
That is the purpose of my exercise at this time. This question is probably the most serious one to face agriculture in my part of Canada, and I make no apology for raising this matter at least once a year and for having this enjoyable debate during the "late show". There is suspicion among the farmers of the Atlantic area, and I think among others as well, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is trying to axe this program. I think the farmers also suspect that the Minister of Agriculture is a doughty proponent of the program, and I hope he will be able to hang in there and see that his colleague does not exercise what would be ridiculous and dangerous parsimony.
I have been talking to people who attended the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, some of them being in the chicken business in Nova Scotia. Of course, chicken is one food that has not changed very much in price over the last few years. Enormous quantities are being produced now and dispensed to the public by such people as Colonel Sanders, Chubby Chicken, and the like. I asked the suppliers of this chicken whether they were getting greater returns for it: the cost must have gone up, so how on earth could they stay in the chicken business? After a long pause one of the most successful ones in Nova Scotia replied, "Well, it must be the feed grain freight assistance that made the difference between having a chicken farm that operates at a profit and one that would have operated at a loss". So it is frightfully important to the livestock industry in Halifax-East Hants and the adjoining farming communities in Nova Scotia.
I think the minister will recognize that it is important that these people receive an answer to the question, if only so that they may plan ahead. Who wants to be

February 4, 1971

ordering extra livestock if suddenly the animals are going to be eating the head off the farmer because the assistance program is not forthcoming or is watered down? I think the minister will recognize the merit in my bringing the question before him at this time. The Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture, in its position paper regarding the report of the federal task force on agriculture, made some points with regard to this problem. I quote from page 6 of this document as follows:
We are amazed over the fact that no mention was made of the transportation problems, especially in the maritime region. Factors such as railway tariffs, transportation facilities, access to markets and systems of agreed charges are the root cause of many problems. A special study should be undertaken to look into this matter and recommendations made for the solution to these problems.
On the following page this statement is made, and perhaps it is a misprint:
We must take great exception to the recommendation that the feed freight assistance program be disconinued by August 1, 1970.
This document was put out on November 1, 1970, so I am at a loss to understand why that particular date appears where it does. In any event, they make the point that Nova Scotia is only 20 per cent self-sufficient in feed grain production, most of which is oats: there is also some barley and mixed grains. They say, "The prospect of self-sufficiency by 1980 is a far removed dream". So I ask the Minister of Agriculture to take that message to the Minister of Finance and tell him to put it in his pipe and smoke it. We are not likely to become self-sufficient in this area, commendable or attractive as that objective might appear to be.
We are one country. In the west we have farmers who are growing grain and doing their darndest to find somebody to buy it. In the east we have farmers who for their livestock or chicken industries desperately need foodstuffs. So I suggest, what is more obvious and practical than to bring the supply to the demand and thus bring health to agriculture at both ends of Canada? Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture two questions. Will the program continue after March 31, 1971? If so, at what level? That is, will the formula be the same?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-INQUIRY AS TO CONTINUATION OF FEED GRAIN FREIGHT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no wish to question the hon. member's right to bring this matter before the House of Commons and to request or demand a reply. However, I do not believe he should purport to be the spokesman for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I am aware of the motions that they accepted and the ones they defeated. I understand they are going to put them in a brief which will be submitted to cabinet. It will be presented by that organization very shortly to the cabinet. However, I want to make it very clear that as yet we have not received that brief based on the resolutions which were accepted and defeated at the recent convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
The hon. member is demanding a yes or no answer. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that in many cases-this is
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion one of them-the most accurate answer cannot be either a categoric yes or no because quite obviously there are anomalies that creep into the system, changes in the freight rates in various zones from one year to the next, and it is our intention in consultation with the farm organizations to review them and adjust them accordingly. I can say to the hon. member that there will be a feed freight assistance program after the end of March 31, 1971. He wants to know how and at what level the expenditures will be. I think he is asking a question that he knows I cannot answer. We have to bring these estimates to Parliament about April 1, at the beginning of the new fiscal year, and when that new fiscal year starts we generally make an announcement of what the rates will be.
Last year, during the course of the year, because of apprehension about the task force's recommendations, we announced that we were prepared to carry on the rates at the existing level to the end of this fiscal year. This year, if we can make the announcement early in the new fiscal year we will do so because it is useful for farmers to have that information.

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-ALBERTA-ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITY FOR DINOSAUR AREA
INDIAN AFFAIRS-ALBERTA-ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITY FOR DINOSAUR AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in raising this matter tonight is in recognition of the fact that on some matters it is impossible to get governments to act, particularly where more than one level of government is involved, except through arousing public opinion. While I realize that within the four walls of this chamber tonight there is not present a very large segment of the Canadian public, nevertheless I hope to make a contribution to the resolving of the issue.
The record of Hansard will show that on January 13 last I sought unanimous consent of the House to move a motion which, if passed, would have resulted in the repatriation to the public realm of the areas of Wood Buffalo National Park alienated under timber lease agreements. In my introductory preface to the motion I indicated that what was going on in that national park was a complete negation of the basic terms of the national parks trust, and that it was incompatible with the general administration of national parks in Canada. As a matter of fact, what precipitated my decision to move that motion which, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, did not get the unanimous consent of the House, was the story which appeared in that day's issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail, a Canadian Press story which was headlined, "National Park Being Stripped-Forester Says", the forester being one of the people involved in the administration in Alberta of the national parks.
Since that time I have seen a rather interesting cartoon depicting the buffalo trying to graze around in a sea of stumps. The implication was that this was not a very satisfactory habitat for wood buffalo. As a follow-up to that and as a result of the report of the attempt to have that motion dealt with in the House, a statement was issued by officials of the parks branch here in Ottawa to the effect that among other things the parks branch did
February 4, 1971

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion not have the kind of money that would be necessary to repatriate these areas which were under timber lease. It mentioned that they had spent money buying out timber leases in Jasper and Banff National Parks. As a followup, I asked a question of the minister which Your Honour thought should be placed on the Order Paper. In Hansard this rather ambiguous heading appears over the question, "Alberta-Establishment of facility in dinosaur area".

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-ALBERTA-ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITY FOR DINOSAUR AREA
speechtext: That refers to Liberals.

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-ALBERTA-ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITY FOR DINOSAUR AREA
speechtext:
That heading does not explain what kind of facility is meant. An hon. member near me has made a remark agout the kind of dinosaur in Alberta that I perhaps had in mind. However, Mr. Speaker, the question is a serious one and I was not altogether ignorant of what was involved when I asked it. As a matter of fact, the minister had an opportunity or replying as a result of a related question asked by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). He pointed out that timber is being cut in Wood Buffalo park and went on to say, as reported at page 2447 of Hansard:
-we are presently negotiating with the government of Alberta to establish new limits, as far as Wood Buffalo park is concerned, which would enable us to obtain in exchange the areas where dinosaurs are still to be found, in Alberta.
I think the minister's statement was a little ambiguous. I am sure members of the House realize that we were talking about rare dinosaur bones and not about living and roaming dinosaurs. The point at issue is this: When are the two governments going to get together and really do something about this matter? I remind the House that on April 23 of last year a minister of the Alberta government, Hon. A. O. Fimrite, appeared before the committee and presented a brief. He was questioned by the members of the Northern Affairs Committee on the subject. I refer to the issue of April 23. At page 12:42 Mr. Fimrite explains one section of the brief which says this:
If Wood Buffalo Park was fulfilling the function of a national park, matters would be much different, as a viable national park would be served by road or rail and significant facilities would exist to serve the visiting public. The operation of a national park similar in scope and attractiveness to either Banff or Jasper would be a substantial asset to the province. Such, however, is not the case.
He went on to say that not all national parks have the same kinds of attractions. He continued:
I would give as an example the Dinosaur Park in Alberta in which the federal government has indicated an interest for an exchange with Wood Buffalo park. The provincial government is prepared to consider this suggestion because this area does lend itself for a park of a type which would be the only area in Canada with this particular attraction.
This was said last April, almost one year ago, yet the other day in the House the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) said that the government is negotiating with the government of Alberta. I know that discussions between the two governments went on for a long time before the minister of the Alberta government made that statement before the committee. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, in Wood Buffalo park there is a basic violation with respect to national parks trust.
I suggest it is time the two governments got together, reached agreement and established new national parks in the province of Alberta. They should redefine the Wood Buffalo park's areas so that if there is logging in some areas it will be done under management and conservation arrangements and under the law of the province of Alberta.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-ALBERTA-ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITY FOR DINOSAUR AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help feeling that I am in an Alice in Wonderland atmosphere tonight. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was somewhat vilified in the questions asked by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). I did not have the opportunity of responding to their questions. However, I now have the opportunity to respond to a question.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) devoted approximately 80 per cent of his time to timber operations in Wood Buffalo National Park. The question on the adjournment debate is the establishment of a dinosaur park in the province of Alberta. I am very pleased to have the opportunity on behalf of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) to respond to this very important question affecting the province of Alberta.
The desirability of including Dinosaur provincial park in the national parks system has been discussed with the province of Alberta since 1963. A joint federal-provincial survey of the area in June, 1966, confirmed that the scenic and scientific values are sufficiently significant to warrant designating this area as a national park. This area is reputed to be the richest bed of dinosaur fossils in North America, with well over 200 finds since the first fossil was found in 1912. The exposure of a large portion of the Oldman geologic formation in this area has resulted in an extensive example of badland topography. Within this park the prairie vegetation gives way to a dry vegetation type, providing a unique combination of plants and animals not portrayed in any national park of Canada.
Acquisition is directly connected with federal-provincial discussions on Wood Buffalo National Park. Alberta has requested the release of all Wood Buffalo Natioal Park lands in the province to permit resource exploitation. Successive federal administrations have rejected this request but have expressed a willingness to consider an exchange of some lands in Wood Buffalo for other areas of high quality in the province. This exchange would not necessarily be on an acre-for-acre basis. It is

February 4, 1971

an express condition that national park values in Wood Buffalo be retained within any reduced boundaries.
The federal position was reiterated by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to the provincial minister responsible, Hon. J. Donovan Ross, at a meeting with him in March, 1970. At that time Dr. Ross
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
was asked to submit a proposal indicating the lands within Wood Buffalo of interest to them and which could form the basis for an exchange of lands. That proposal has not yet been received.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10:30 p.m.
